title: Сотейник в сейфе  (The Sauté Pan in the Safe)

segments.t: Back in the office at Claude Monet, German takes kitchen security to a ridiculous extreme by locking the copper sauté pan inside a heavy metal safe and pocketing the key.
Вам не кажется, что это перебор?
От него можно ожидать чего угодно.
Я всё-таки возьму ключики от сейфа.
Он не станет заниматься такой ерундой.
Let's go through Vika and German's exchange around the office safe.
'And your sauté pan is fine.' Vika presents a natural attitude in the conversation, anchoring the Russian line on "soteynik" ("pan") and "poryadke" ("order") without extra filler.
Вам не кажется, что это перебор?

'Does it not seem to you that this is overkill?' Vika wonders dryly from the start, using "kazhetsya" (from "kazatsya", "it seems, I think") alongside "perebor" ("too much, overkill") to shape the meaning.
'He steals a defenseless sauté pan!' German presents a warm footing across the room, combining "kradyot" ("is stealing") and "bezzashchitnyy" ("defenseless") so the key meaning lands right away.
'And these are security measures.' German establishes a calm attitude in the scene, joining "mery" ("measures") to "bezopasnosti" ("safety, security") so every word pulls its weight.
'Excuse me, what safe is this?' German questions candidly without a pause, combining "prostite" ("excuse me") and "seyf" ("safe") so the key meaning lands right away.
'It was left over from the old owners.' Vika strikes a sharp rhythm as they talk, joining "ostalsya" ("remained") to "starykh" ("old") so every word pulls its weight.
'I do not use it.' Vika offers an easygoing approach at this moment, putting "polzuyus" ("I am taking advantage") alongside "ya" ("I") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Well, I will use it, give me the keys.' German shares a wry angle in their talk, pairing "popolzuyus" ("keys") with "dayte" ("give") so the "-sya" ending carries the action.
'Now that is another matter.' German sustains a frank style at once, building the phrase around "drugoye" ("another, other") and "delo" ("matter") for a crisp, natural delivery.
'Do you think Viktor will try again?' Vika tests candidly without a pause, joining "dumayete" ("think") to "snova" ("again") so every word pulls its weight.
От него можно ожидать чего угодно.
'You can expect anything at all from him.' German shares a serious footing as the scene unfolds, weaving "mozhno" ("may, can") together with "ozhidat" ("to expect") just the way native speakers do.
Я всё-таки возьму ключики от сейфа.
'I will take the spare keys to the safe after all.' Vika sets a frank tack right away, leaning on "vozmu" ("will get") before closing the thought with "klyuchiki" ("little key").
'You do not use it, do you?' German tests boldly toward Vika here, leaning on "polzuyetes" ("are taking advantage of") before closing the thought with "vy" ("you").
Он не станет заниматься такой ерундой.

'He will not bother with such nonsense.' Vika chooses a candid footing in the room, linking "stanet" ("will become"), "zanimatsya" ("to be busy with"), and "yerundoy" ("nonsense") in one brisk exchange. Now let's hear the whole scene again from start to finish.
Вам не кажется, что это перебор?
От него можно ожидать чего угодно.
Я всё-таки возьму ключики от сейфа.
Он не станет заниматься такой ерундой.
That wraps up this scene as german locks the reclaimed copper sauté pan inside an old office safe to keep Barinov away from it, and Vika slyly asks to borrow the spare keys. See you next time!
